title: Intel Confirms Fresh Layoffs in Data Center Unit Ahead of Quarterly Earnings
excerpt: The chipmaker is cutting jobs in its Data Center and AI Group as part of a broader restructuring, days before reporting second-quarter results on July 23.
body:
Intel has confirmed a new round of layoffs targeting its Data Center and AI Group (DCG), the division responsible for server processors and custom AI chips, as the semiconductor giant continues a sweeping restructuring under CEO Lip-Bu Tan.

The company declined to specify how many employees would be affected or provide regional breakdowns. Intel spokesperson Chelsea Vera said the cuts are part of a broader effort to streamline the business.

"Our Data Center Group is aligning its organization to ensure it has the right roles and skills in place to position the business for long-term success."

— Chelsea Vera, Intel spokesperson

The layoffs were first reported by The Oregonian and confirmed by multiple outlets on Monday. They come just days before Intel is scheduled to report second-quarter results after US markets close on Thursday, July 23.

A Shrinking Workforce

The latest cuts extend what has become one of the most aggressive restructuring campaigns in the US semiconductor industry. Intel's global headcount has declined from approximately 125,000 at the end of 2023 to around 78,500 as of the first quarter of 2026 — a reduction of more than 46,000 employees in roughly two and a half years.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=lKwejIaKzvU

CEO Lip-Bu Tan, who took the reins in March 2025, launched a 20% workforce reduction shortly after assuming leadership, with a stated goal of cutting $1.5 billion in costs and building a leaner, more engineering-focused culture. The company shed roughly 15,000 positions in 2024 alone.

In Oregon, Intel's largest employment base, the workforce peaked at about 23,000 in early 2024. By 2025, that figure had fallen to around 20,200 before an additional 3,200 layoffs were announced. Intel has declined to disclose current headcount in the state, though local reporting suggests it may still employ around 17,000 people there. In Arizona, roughly 800 of the company's 9,600 employees were let go in 2025. No new WARN Act notices had been filed in Arizona as of Tuesday.

Cutting Where Revenue Is Growing

What makes these layoffs unusual is that they target one of Intel's strongest-performing divisions. The Data Center and AI Group posted revenue growth of 22% year-on-year in the first quarter of 2026, driven by expanding demand for server CPUs as data centre buildouts accelerate worldwide. Intel's PC processor business, by contrast, grew just 1% over the same period.

RBC Capital, in a note ahead of Thursday's earnings call, maintained a Sector Perform rating on Intel with an $80 price target. The brokerage expects Intel to deliver roughly a 5% revenue beat for the second quarter, with gross margins coming in 1 to 2 percentage points above consensus. RBC identified Intel's server CPU business as a key source of strength, forecasting double-digit volume growth through the rest of 2026.

Intel shares rose approximately 5% in pre-market trading on Tuesday following the layoff reports, with the stock trading near $98. The market appeared to read the cuts as a sign of continued cost discipline rather than business weakness.

Diaspora Watch

Intel employs thousands of Indian-origin engineers across its US campuses, particularly in Oregon, Arizona, and California. Workforce reductions of this scale at a major H-1B visa sponsor raise concerns for Indian tech workers, who face compressed timelines to find new employment or risk losing immigration status.

What Comes Next

Thursday's earnings call will be closely watched for several reasons. Investors want specifics: how deep the DCG cuts will go, what restructuring charges Intel will book, and whether the company can maintain the data centre unit's growth momentum with fewer people.

The call will also serve as an update on Intel Foundry Services, the contract chipmaking business that has been a drag on profitability but represents a central pillar of Tan's long-term strategy. Progress on the Intel 18A manufacturing process and any new customer commitments will be key signals.

Wall Street currently expects Intel to report earnings of approximately $0.22 per share on $14.45 billion in revenue for the June quarter, according to Koyfin data. Whether Intel can beat those numbers while absorbing yet another round of restructuring costs will define the market's near-term outlook for the stock.
